hints: Focus on oxidation numbers, since oxidation and reduction are all about a rise or fall in oxidation number.
Work out the oxidation number of chlorine in $\text{Cl}_2$, in $\text{HOCl}$ and in $\text{Cl}^-$, remembering H is +1 and O is -2 in $\text{HOCl}$.
Check if one element both increases and decreases in oxidation number, and see what happens to hydrogen to confirm it stays at +1 throughout.
walkthrough:
**Assign oxidation numbers to chlorine**

Think of oxidation numbers as a book-keeping tool. In an element, it is 0, so in $\text{Cl}_2$ each Cl is 0.

$$\text{Cl in Cl}_2 = 0$$

**Find chlorine in the products**

In $\text{HOCl}$, H is +1 and O is -2, so Cl must be +1 to give a neutral molecule. In $\text{Cl}^-$ it is simply -1.

$$\text{Cl in HOCl} = +1, \quad \text{Cl in Cl}^- = -1$$

**Compare and spot disproportionation**

One Cl atom goes from 0 to +1, that is oxidation (loss of electrons). The other goes from 0 to -1, that is reduction (gain of electrons).

$$0 \to +1 \text{ (oxidised) and } 0 \to -1 \text{ (reduced)}$$

**Check hydrogen for completeness**

Hydrogen is +1 in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, +1 in $\text{HOCl}$ and +1 in $\text{H}^+$. It does not change, so it is neither oxidised nor reduced. This confirms chlorine is both oxidised and reduced.

options.A: Correct. Chlorine starts at 0 in Cl2, then splits to +1 in HOCl (oxidised) and -1 in Cl- (reduced). When the same element is both oxidised and reduced, we call it disproportionation.
options.B: Incorrect. It is true chlorine is oxidised to +1 in HOCl, but it is also reduced to -1 in Cl-. This option misses the reduction half of the disproportionation.
options.C: Incorrect. Hydrogen stays at +1 in H2O, in HOCl and in H+. With no change in oxidation number, hydrogen is neither oxidised nor reduced.
options.D: Incorrect. Hydrogen does not change oxidation number at all, so it cannot be described as oxidised. Students sometimes confuse H+ formation with oxidation, but oxidation needs an increase in oxidation number.
